maps.title: The world of the first Christians
maps.intro: The places that matter most in this era, from Jerusalem to Rome. Region names are the Roman ones used in Acts and Paul's letters.

maps.title: First journey
maps.intro: Acts says the church at Antioch sent out Barnabas and Paul. They crossed Cyprus, then went inland to cities in the Roman province of Galatia, in the regions Acts calls Pisidia and Lycaonia, and came back the same way.

maps.title: Second journey
maps.intro: Acts says Paul set out again with Silas, revisited the churches inland, then crossed by sea into Macedonia and Greece for the first time.

maps.intro: Acts says Paul spent a long stay in Ephesus, went back through Macedonia and Greece, then sailed down the coast toward Jerusalem.

maps.intro: Acts says Paul, now a prisoner, was sent to Rome by ship. A storm drove the ship west for two weeks until it wrecked on Malta.

maps.title: Cities named in the sources for this era
maps.intro: The cities that appear most often in the writings of AD 100 to 313, from Antioch in the east to Carthage in the west. Lyons and Vienne in Gaul, where Irenaeus was bishop, lie off the western edge of this map.

maps.title: Ignatius on the road to Rome
maps.intro: Eusebius says Ignatius was sent from Syria to Rome under military guard, and that he wrote from Smyrna and from Troas. Polycarp's letter shows the Philippians had seen him pass. Nothing records the rest of the way, so the lines between these stops are straight and show only the order.

maps.title: The church around AD 400
maps.intro: The main churches and cities of the empire around the time of the councils of the fourth century. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Churches and kingdoms about 600
maps.intro: The churches in the era of Gregory the Great and Justinian: Rome and Ravenna, the eastern patriarchates, Carthage, and the new English church. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: The English church and the East, about 700
maps.intro: Whitby, Lindisfarne and Canterbury in the north and west, with the eastern cities of the councils. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: The Carolingian world and the schism
maps.intro: The Frankish kingdoms around Aachen and Verdun, the papacy in Rome, and the eastern and northern frontiers. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Reform and crusade, about 1100
maps.intro: The reforming papacy and its opponents, the monasteries of Cluny and Cîteaux, and the road to Jerusalem. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: The schism and the councils
maps.intro: Avignon and Rome, the councils of Constance and Basel, and the frontier with the Ottomans at Kosovo. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Europe in the fifteenth century
maps.intro: The councils of Basel and Florence, the Renaissance courts of Italy, Constantinople and the Ottoman frontier in the Balkans, and the edge of Muscovy. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Religion in Europe about 1555
maps.intro: After the Peace of Augsburg, the German princes chose their religion, and the Reformed churches held Geneva, Scotland and parts of the Netherlands. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: The Thirty Years' War, 1618 to 1648
maps.intro: The war began in Bohemia and spread across the empire, drawing in Denmark, Sweden and France. Westphalia, where the peace was made, is shown in the north-west. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Confessions in Europe about 1700
maps.intro: Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed and Orthodox lands after the wars of religion, with the Habsburg and Ottoman frontiers. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Europe in 1789
maps.intro: The states of Europe on the eve of the French Revolution: the Estates-General at Versailles, the Habsburg and Prussian courts, the Russian Holy Synod, and the Jesuit suppression. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Europe after the Congress of Vienna, 1815
maps.intro: The restored states of Europe, with the Papal States returned to the pope and the Holy Alliance in place. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: The Papal States, 1789 to 1870
maps.intro: Rome and its territory in the years between the Revolution and the fall of Rome. The papal enclaves in France (Avignon and the Venaissin) were lost in 1790 and the Papal States were occupied in 1809 and again in 1860 and 1870. Boundaries are simplified and approximate.

maps.title: The Balkans and the Ottoman East, 1821 to 1870
maps.intro: Greece, the Danubian principalities, the Bulgarian Exarchate of 1870, and the Ottoman capital. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: The Ottoman Balkans and the Congress of Berlin, 1878
maps.intro: The Balkans and eastern Anatolia after the Russo-Turkish war, as settled at the Congress of Berlin. Boundaries are simplified and approximate.

maps.title: Europe in 1914
maps.intro: The great powers on the eve of the First World War, with the Ottoman lands and the Armenian provinces. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Europe, 1933 to 1945
maps.intro: Germany, Italy, Spain and the Soviet Union, with the places where the churches met the regimes: Rome, Berlin, Barmen and Flossenbürg. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Europe divided, 1950
maps.intro: The Iron Curtain across Europe in 1950, with the Soviet-controlled churches to the east and the free churches to the west. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: Central and Eastern Europe, 1956 to 1989
maps.intro: The churches of the Soviet bloc and their neighbours, from the Hungarian uprising of 1956 to the revolutions of 1989. Boundaries are simplified.

maps.title: The First Crusade, 1096 to 1099
maps.intro: The route of the crusading armies from Constantinople to Jerusalem, with the battles and sieges that marked it. The route is simplified and straight between places; the battle sites and dates are not yet checked.

stops.note: Besieged from May 1097 and surrendered in June to the Byzantine emperor, not to the crusaders

maps.title: The Third Crusade, 1189 to 1192
maps.intro: Richard I's route from Sicily and Cyprus to Acre and along the coast, with the battles of Arsuf and Jaffa. Frederick Barbarossa's army took the inland route, and he drowned in a river in Cilicia in 1190. Hattin, the battle of 1187 that began the crusade, is marked for background. The routes are simplified, and the sites and dates are not yet checked.

stops.name: Acre
stops.note: Besieged from 1189 and surrendered in July 1191 to the forces of Philip II and Richard I; it becomes the crusaders' base
Battle on 7 September 1191, where Richard's army defeats Saladin's forces in an attack along the coast
Saladin attacks the city in 1192, and Richard's army holds it in the summer; a truce follows in September, and Richard does not reach Jerusalem

maps.title: The Fourth Crusade, 1202 to 1204
maps.intro: The fleet route from Venice by way of Zara, Corfu and Modon to Constantinople, with the places where the crusade became a war against Christians (Zara in 1202, and Constantinople in 1203 and 1204), and Negroponte, taken after the sack. The route is simplified and straight between places; the sites and dates are not yet checked.

stops.note: Taken in November 1202 for Venice, though the pope had forbidden attacks on Christian cities; the crusade is diverted

stops.name: Negroponte
stops.note: Taken by Venice after the sack, as part of the division of the empire (1204, to check)
